title: The ten-dollar game
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: If you are offered a split, what is your real aim?

Jose described a class exercise from the book, the ultimatum game: people are in pairs as a proposer and an acceptor. The proposer offers a number of dollars; if the acceptor agrees, the acceptor gets the offer and the proposer keeps the rest, and if not, they lose it all.
He ran it in the class with ten dollars, and said the money had been given to the players, so they could lose it.
A student asked how both could win: invest the ten dollars together and split the return, perhaps sixty-forty, and talk about how to distribute the gains.
Another said: the natural thing is to split the difference, but I am not sure that is our aim in this negotiation. If there is no set timeline, I continuously hold my position until they give up.

Jose said that you have to be careful with the word fair, because it is a fair price and then you think: wait, wait, wait. He said the proposer needs you, because he has to do the deal with you or lose all the money.

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write a split you could be offered.
Write what you really want from it.
Write a way both sides could win.
Write what the other side loses if there is no deal.
Write how you will use the word fair.

check.q: What are the two roles in the game?
What did a student say the natural move is?
What did Jose say about the word fair?

recap: Know your real aim. Look for a way both can win. Be careful with fair.
